title: Hijab, many choices
hookLine: the hijab worn as devotion, with views and practices that vary

lines: A PIN, A MIRROR, A MOMENT.
cards: A pin between the teeth. A mirror by the door. A length of soft fabric wrapped once, tucked, pinned, checked.
The woman doing it is also finding her keys and telling her son to put his shoes on. To a stranger it might look like a statement. To her it's part of leaving the house.
Maybe her grandmother wore one; maybe she never did. Either way, this woman decided for herself. Her sister, beside her, doesn't wear one at all.
Same family, same faith, same mirror. And in the Qur'an, the word for that fabric means something else.

teach.h: IN THE QUR'AN, HIJAB IS A CURTAIN.
teach.b: Day one hundred thirty-nine asked why hijab; today, the word and its readings. In the Qur'an, hijab doesn't name a headscarf. It means a screen or a curtain.
In surah al-Ahzab, people who need to ask the Prophet's wives for something are told, in paraphrase, to ask from behind a curtain, and that curtain is a hijab. Then the verses about dress.
In surah al-Nur, believing men are told first to lower their gaze and guard their modesty. Then believing women are told the same, and to draw their khimar, their head-covering, over their chests.

Another verse in al-Ahzab speaks of women drawing their outer garments around them so they may be recognized and not troubled. The headscarf people call hijab today comes from how these verses have been read.
Scholars of the classical schools, Sunni and Shia, read them as requiring a woman to cover her hair in front of men outside her close family.

teach.h: READINGS: DUTY, OR SHAPED BY EACH.
teach.b: Some contemporary Muslim writers read them as a call to modesty that each woman shapes for herself. Muslim women hold both views, and speak for both. The practice varies too.
Some wear it from childhood, some start as adults, some cover only for prayer, some wear it and later stop, some start again.
Styles change from Jakarta to Cairo to Dearborn. And the reasons women who wear it give are their own: devotion to Allah, obedience, a reminder through the day, identity, privacy.
Some who see it as required still describe it as something offered to Allah, a duty taken up with the heart.

how: Muslim women who wear hijab cover their hair in front of men outside their close family, in styles that vary by region and taste; classical scholars teach it as required, some contemporary writers read the verses as a call to modesty, and women's own practice and reasons vary.

o: a curtain in the Qur'an; today, a head-covering
a mat spread on the floor for the daily prayer

games.q: in al-Ahzab, people need to ask the Prophet's wives for something. how are they told to ask?
o: from behind a curtain, a hijab.
games.why: they are told to ask from behind a curtain: that is the word hijab in the Qur'an.

practice: Bring to mind a woman you've seen wearing a hijab, on a train, in a store, on a screen, and notice the first thought that came with the picture; don't argue with it, just set it down like a bag.
Then picture her as the hook did: keys, a son's shoes, a moment at the mirror. If you pray, ask for good for her in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Hijab. In the Qur'an, a screen or curtain; today, the name for a Muslim woman's head-covering, with views and practices that vary. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: a choice of devotion. Her reasons are hers to give. Tomorrow, young Muslims.
